read: full (abstract, introduction, related work, setup pp2-3, automatic evaluation pp3-5, human evaluation pp5-7, plagiarism p7, discussion and conclusion pp7-8, limitations p9; appendices skimmed, including the agreement appendix)
venue_now: Proceedings of the 16th International Natural Language Generation Conference (INLG 2023), pages 323-351 (p1 header)
what_it_is: An empirical comparison of story generation by GPT-3 (text-davinci-001, prompted with two or three example stories) against fine-tuned story generators (KGGPT2, PROGEN, MTCL, HINT, BART) on three corpora: ROCStories, WritingPrompts and CNN news (pp2-4; p4 Table 1). Stories are scored with reference-based and reference-free automatic metrics and by two groups of human judges, crowdworkers and in-house volunteers, on fluency, coherence, relatedness, logicality and interestingness (pp3-7). GPT-3's stories were rated significantly better than the other systems' and comparable to human-written ones; lexical metrics disagreed with the human ratings; and GPT-3 tended to reproduce real news stories, a form of soft plagiarism (p1; p7; p8).
size: 3 datasets; 6 generation systems; automatic evaluation on 800 ROC, 1,000 WP and 600 CNN contexts (p3); human evaluation on 20 contexts per dataset for each annotator group, 3 annotators per story (pp5-6)
evaluation: reference-based metrics (corpus BLEU, MS-Jaccard, BERTScore, BLEURT, backward BLEU), reference-free metrics (Self-BLEU, Distinct-3, lexical repetition, BARTScore, length), and 1-5 human ratings on five aspects (pp3-6)
human_validation: Crowdworkers on Mechanical Turk and 15 in-house volunteers (14 PhD students, 1 staff member), three ratings per story; the two groups agreed on the main findings (pp5-6); agreement statistics are in an appendix.
contamination_measures: n/a. It does check GPT-3's outputs for plagiarism: iThenticate similarity of 4%, 3% and 14% for ROC, WP and CNN, and a manual check finding 7 of 10 sampled CNN stories based on real news (p7).

engtrace_use.sentence: As LLMs expand into high-stakes engineering workflows, rigorous evaluation of their reasoning capabilities has become paramount (Zhao et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023a). (L45-48)
engtrace_use.explanation: The paper evaluates the quality of generated stories (p1). It does not evaluate reasoning, does not mention engineering, and makes no claim about high-stakes deployment. Its closest content is methodological: human evaluation remains the gold standard for story quality, and lexical metrics agree poorly with it (p8; p9). Cited for the importance of evaluating LLM reasoning in engineering, it implies support the paper does not give.

suggested_wording: In story generation, crowdworkers and in-house judges rated GPT-3's stories as comparable to human-written ones, while lexical reference-based metrics disagreed with those ratings (Xie et al., 2023a).
facts_to_cite: Compares prompted GPT-3 (text-davinci-001) with five fine-tuned story generators on ROCStories, WritingPrompts and CNN news (pp2-4; p4 Table 1).
Human judges, both crowdworkers and in-house, rated GPT-3's stories significantly above the other systems' and comparable to human-written stories (p1 abstract; pp5-6, Tables 4-5).
Lexical automatic metrics correlated weakly with human evaluation, and model-based metrics appeared more reliable (p8 conclusion).
GPT-3 tended to reproduce details of real news stories (7 of 10 sampled CNN stories), raising questions about memorisation (p7).
overlap_with_engtrace: None. Story generation, not reasoning; no gold traces, no step-level evaluation, no engineering, no generated instances. The only shared theme is distrust of reference-based metrics and reliance on human judgement, which EngTrace now addresses with expert-labelled traces (state brief section 3).
notes: Self-citation: Zhuohan Xie is an author of EngTrace and of this paper (citation_context_map C9). An off-topic self-citation in the first sentence of the paper invites a reviewer's objection; the opening claim is better carried by a source that supports it (see zhao2023survey, p61). The paper's memorisation finding (p7) concerns plagiarism in model outputs, not benchmark contamination, so it does not support the contamination framing either.
